meta.product: AI Berkshire — The AI Investment Committee
meta.description: Pre-analyzed companies extracted from real AI Berkshire research reports (four-master committee framework). All figures were cross-validated from 2+ sources and computed with decimal-precision tooling at research time.
meta.disclaimer: Educational research tool. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Not investment advice.

buffett.name: Warren Buffett
buffett.question: What is it worth, and is there a margin of safety?

munger.name: Charlie Munger
munger.question: Invert: how does this company die?

companies.name: Tencent Holdings
companies.verdictLine: A classic case of buying an excellent company at a fair price: WeChat's 1.4B-MAU social moat is nearly unassailable, gross margin rose from 42% to 56% in 4 years, and buybacks are the largest in Hong Kong market history.

duan.thesis: The social network effect is irreplaceable — gaming plus advertising is a twin engine. I hold it heavily myself and call it a non-sellable asset.

buffett.thesis: 56% gross margin, 182.6B RMB free cash flow, HK$112B of buybacks. PE 16x is cheap-ish but not screaming cheap.

munger.thesis: The social moat can't be stormed head-on, but ByteDance is laying siege around the walls — Video Accounts are the biggest growth lever left.

lilu.thesis: Top-tier management, but no visible successor, and being behind ByteDance in consumer AI is the real worry.

conflict.line: Duan calls it a 'non-sellable' forever asset; Li Lu warns the AI application gap versus ByteDance is 5.5x and could demote it from growth stock to value stock.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: Fourteen hundred million people open WeChat every day. Alibaba tried to copy it. ByteDance tried. Both failed. That is the whole thesis.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: Nobody storms the castle, agreed. But ByteDance isn't storming it — it's rerouting the ad budgets around it. Siege warfare works too.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: While you two argue, the company bought back HK$112 billion of its own stock. At 16 times earnings I don't need heroic assumptions.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: One caution: their consumer AI assistant trails ByteDance's by 5.5x in usage. If AI redefines the super-app, today's moat maps may be obsolete. I still pass it — with monitoring.

tieredAdvice.logic: PE 16x + Video Accounts upside + buyback support
Wait for quarterly proof of Video Accounts monetization
Wait for PE under 14x before sizing up

inversion: AI-native super-app displaces WeChat as the OS of Chinese daily life (low probability, high impact)
Regulatory re-tightening on gaming or platform economics
Succession vacuum after the current leadership generation
companies.mirrorTest: Deepest moat in Chinese internet; margins expanding; management returns cash aggressively; price is fair, not euphoric; biggest risk is losing the AI application race.

companies.name: PDD Holdings (Pinduoduo / Temu)
companies.verdictLine: A hyper-efficient cash printing machine (ROE 31%, $59.5B net cash, ex-cash PE ~6.3x) — but the moat is narrower than it looks, Temu faces structural tariff walls, and management returns zero cash. Cheap, but not 'great'. Mid-size position at most.

duan.thesis: Efficiency-driven, not brand-driven. Scale is the only real moat here; 'cheap' is a brand discount, not a brand premium.

buffett.thesis: Textbook balance sheet, free cash flow with near-zero capex, and an ex-cash PE of 6.3x. This is a cash machine priced for decline.

munger.thesis: Four-way knife fight. Douyin built 4 trillion GMV in three years — the moat is shallower than everyone thinks. Tariffs are the wild card.

lilu.thesis: Management culture is a hidden liability, global regulatory risk is extreme, zero buybacks, zero dividends. I cannot see 10-year certainty. Veto on heavy positions.

conflict.line: Buffett: 'a cash machine at 6.3x ex-cash earnings — genuinely cheap.' Li Lu: 'no 10-year certainty and disappointing capital allocation — cheapness doesn't cure that.' This is the widest split in the entire coverage universe.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: Strip out the cash and you're paying about six times earnings for a business earning 31% on equity. I've bought far worse for far more.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: And what do the owners get? No dividend. No buyback. $59 billion sits there while the controlling culture treats minority shareholders as spectators. Price is not the problem — certainty is.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: Invert it: Douyin went from zero to 4 trillion GMV in three years. If the moat were real, that shouldn't have been possible.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: It is a good operation, not yet a good business. When 'cheapest' is your promise, the customer's loyalty lasts exactly until someone is cheaper.

tieredAdvice.logic: Ex-cash PE 6.3x, historic-low valuation
Temu tariff overhang is the key structural variable

tieredAdvice.priceBand: Consider below $75 or after an HK listing
tieredAdvice.logic: Fails the 10-year certainty test; wait for Temu profitability proof

inversion: Global tariff walls permanently cap Temu's economics
Douyin/JD price war compresses take rates at home
Governance discount becomes permanent — cash never reaches shareholders
companies.mirrorTest: Extraordinary efficiency and cash generation at a single-digit ex-cash multiple; but narrow moat, tariff exposure, and shareholder-unfriendly capital allocation mean it can be a position, never a conviction holding.

companies.name: Pop Mart International
companies.verdictLine: A money-printing consumer platform (72% gross margin, 55% ROE, zero debt) run by a 5-star founder at PE 13x — but the core question 'can story-less IP stay evergreen?' has no certain answer. LABUBU is 38% of revenue. Small position, watch closely.

duan.thesis: The 'record label for IP' model is excellent, but IP concentration is too high — story-less IP is naturally short-lived.

buffett.thesis: 72% gross margin, 35% net margin, 55% ROE at 13x earnings. The +259% inventory build is the one yellow light on a beautiful statement.

munger.thesis: Remember Funko. Remember Beanie Babies. In all of history, exactly one story-less IP stayed evergreen: Hello Kitty. Base rates matter more than vibes.

lilu.thesis: Wang Ning is a top-tier founder — five consecutive correct contrarian calls, and deliberately slowing growth is wisdom. Still, I put evergreen probability at only 30–40%.

conflict.line: Buffett sees a debt-free machine at 13x earnings; Munger sees Funko and Beanie Babies in the rear-view mirror and asks why this time is different.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: You rarely get 55% returns on equity with no leverage at 13 times earnings. The financials are not the debate.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: Correct — the debate is mortality. Toy fads die young. One exception in history, Hello Kitty. Betting on the second exception needs humility.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: The founder is the hedge. Wang Ning owns 48.7%, made five contrarian calls in a row correctly, and is deliberately slowing the LABUBU frenzy. That is rare discipline.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: Good business today. Whether it is a good business in ten years depends on de-LABUBU-ing successfully. Size the position to that uncertainty.

tieredAdvice.logic: Founder quality + financials justify participation

tieredAdvice.priceBand: Add only if non-LABUBU IP revenue share rises
tieredAdvice.logic: Committee's central case: buy-and-watch, not conviction
30–40% evergreen probability is below the certainty bar

inversion: LABUBU cools and no successor IP emerges (the Funko path)
Inventory build (+259%) turns into markdown pressure
Fad-driven overseas expansion overshoots then retrenches
companies.mirrorTest: Exceptional founder, exceptional unit economics, one concentrated fragile asset: the IP itself. Until the portfolio de-concentrates, this is a position sized for being wrong.

companies.name: Meta Platforms
companies.verdictLine: Core business is superb and the competitive position is proven; the only major variable is whether the enormous AI capex earns its keep. Buy on pullbacks, cap at 5–8% of portfolio.

duan.thesis: The core business is excellent; the return on massive capex still has to be proven, year after year.

buffett.thesis: Top-shelf financials at a modest valuation. Capex is the single big swing factor in owner earnings.

munger.thesis: The competitive landscape is extremely favorable and the moat is deep and already validated.

lilu.thesis: Outstanding but aggressive management — capital allocation needs continuous monitoring, not blind trust.

conflict.line: Munger rates the moat a rare 5 stars; Duan withholds the fifth star until the AI capex proves it can compound owner value rather than consume it.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: Three billion daily users and the ad machine keeps compounding. The competition mostly shot itself.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: A great business, yes. But tens of billions a year into AI infrastructure is a promise, not yet a return.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: As long as the core printer funds the bets and the multiple stays modest, I can live with ambition.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: Founder control cuts both ways. Watch the capex-to-return cycle every quarter; conviction here must be earned annually.

tieredAdvice.logic: Moat validated, AI optionality free-ish at current multiple
Capex uncertainty argues for a cap on sizing

tieredAdvice.action: Half position, add on capex ROI proof
tieredAdvice.logic: Wait for evidence AI spend converts to earnings

inversion: AI capex cycle peaks with returns below cost of capital
Regulatory action against ad targeting economics
Attention shift to a platform Meta cannot buy or copy
companies.mirrorTest: Validated moat, elite financials, one honest uncertainty — whether the AI build-out is an investment or a tax. Size accordingly.

companies.name: Uber Technologies
companies.verdictLine: A two-sided network with 76% ride-share dominance, $9.8B FCF growing 18%, at 13x PE — clearly cheap for the growth, but autonomous-vehicle uncertainty is exactly why. Watchlist; buy dips at 3–5% sizing.

duan.thesis: Two-sided network with cross-business leverage and an asset-light model; delivery is the weaker leg.

buffett.thesis: $9.8B of free cash flow, 18% growth, improving margins, 13x earnings. The market is charging a fear discount.

munger.thesis: 76% share in mobility and an underrated membership moat in Uber One. Dominance is real.

lilu.thesis: Dara executed a remarkable turnaround with real capital discipline, but the autonomous-vehicle bet is a large unproven outlay.

conflict.line: Buffett says 13x for an 18%-growth platform is plainly mispriced; Li Lu answers that the AV transition is precisely the kind of decade-scale uncertainty that justifies the discount.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: Thirteen times earnings for a dominant network growing free cash flow at eighteen percent. Somebody in this market is wrong.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: The discount has a name: autonomy. If robotaxis commoditize the supply side, today's driver network is a stranded asset.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: Or the aggregator wins either way — Uber doesn't need to own the robots, just the demand. That's the underrated scenario.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: Platform is good, mobility is great, delivery is ordinary. Buy the whole only when the price pays you for the weakest part.

tieredAdvice.logic: Valuation discount vs growth is unusually wide
Committee central case: watchlist-to-position on weakness
Wait for clarity on the AV partnership economics

inversion: Robotaxi players vertically integrate demand and bypass the aggregator
Regulatory reclassification of drivers compresses margins
Delivery price war resumes and burns the cash engine
companies.mirrorTest: Dominant network, real cash flow, cheap multiple, one existential question mark (autonomy). A position you rent with discipline, not marry.

companies.name: Mastercard
companies.verdictLine: A toll road on global commerce: 45.7% net margin, 43% ROIC, five stacked moats. The business is 5 stars; the 29x price is 3 stars. Top-tier company at a full price — wait for your pitch.

duan.thesis: An asset-light duopoly collecting tolls with near-zero marginal cost. This is what a perfect business model looks like.

buffett.thesis: 45.7% net margin, 43% ROIC, 109% FCF conversion — a genuine money machine. The statement almost audits itself.

munger.thesis: Network effects, switching costs, regulatory barriers, data assets, brand trust — five moats stacked. Disruption stories keep dying at its gates.

lilu.thesis: Management is embracing stablecoins and agentic commerce rather than hiding from them — the right posture. Price, not risk, is the constraint.

conflict.line: Everyone loves the business; the argument is the ticket price. 29x earnings needs 15%+ growth to keep working — and it trades at a 13% premium to Visa.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: If I could own only one business model on earth, a payments toll road is on the shortlist.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: So would I — at a price. Twenty-nine times earnings prices in years of flawless execution. Wonderful company, full ticket.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: The stablecoin obituary for card networks has been written five times. Each time the networks absorbed the disruptor. I expect a sixth.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: No red lines anywhere. My only note: patience is a position too. Full-price quality rewards those who wait for the wobble.

tieredAdvice.action: Small starter, add on any derating
tieredAdvice.logic: Quality this high rarely gets cheap; average in slowly
The business earns 5 stars, the price earns 3
Do not pay a premium to Visa without a reason

inversion: Regulated interchange caps spread globally
Stablecoin rails finally bypass the four-party model at scale
Growth decelerates below the 15% the multiple demands
companies.mirrorTest: One of the world's best businesses at a price that already says so. The risk isn't the company; it's the entry point.

companies.name: Adobe
companies.verdictLine: One of the best business models in creative software at its cheapest valuation in a decade (19x PE, 10x FCF). The discount exists for two nameable reasons — CEO transition and AI disruption anxiety — and the committee judges both survivable. Buy in tranches, 3–5%.

duan.thesis: Subscriptions plus switching costs plus industry-standard status — though the edges of the franchise are being nibbled.

buffett.thesis: 29.5% net margin, 42% FCF margin, $10B+ of cash flow, at the lowest multiple in ten years. Fear is doing the discounting for us.

munger.thesis: The core moat is wide; the AI-disruption thesis is real enough to monitor but so far eats the edges, not the core.

lilu.thesis: Narayen was excellent and is leaving; an undefined succession is the largest short-term risk on the sheet.

conflict.line: Buffett sees a decade-low price on a fortress cash machine; Li Lu reminds the room that fortress plus leadership vacuum has burned value investors before.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: Ten times free cash flow for the industry standard in creative work. The last time it was this cheap was a different decade.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: Cheap for reasons: the architect of the subscription pivot is walking out the door, and nobody knows who inherits the AI war.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: Invert: if generative AI truly killed Photoshop, you'd see it in churn first. You don't — you see it in headlines.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: Professionals don't switch tools that their whole workflow, and their whole industry, standardizes on. Not quickly. Buy slowly, watch churn.

tieredAdvice.logic: Decade-low valuation with intact core moat
CEO transition argues against a lump-sum entry
Leadership clarity is the cheap catalyst to wait for

inversion: AI-native tools convert the next generation of creators before Adobe converts its base to Firefly
A weak external CEO hire triggers strategy churn
Enterprise seat growth quietly turns negative
companies.mirrorTest: Fortress economics, decade-low price, two nameable fears (succession, AI) — both watchable with clear tripwires. That's what a value setup looks like.

companies.name: Novo Nordisk
companies.verdictLine: A quality asset in its difficult season: 33% net margin and 21% ROIC at a 10x PE that assumes the growth engine died permanently — contradicted by oral Wegovy's momentum. But Eli Lilly's product edge is real. Tracking position 2–3%; size up only on CagriSema approval.

duan.thesis: GLP-1 is a superb franchise with subscription-like chronic dosing — but the company is becoming one of two, no longer the only one.

buffett.thesis: 33% net margins, 21% ROIC, and a 10x PE at a historic extreme. The market is pricing a permanent stall; the pipeline disagrees.

munger.thesis: Lilly's product is currently stronger and holds ~60% US share. But invert the pessimism: the market is big enough for two fat duopolists.

lilu.thesis: New CEO pointing the right direction, execution still early. CagriSema's FDA decision is the swing variable — that's a coin you don't have to flip with a big position.

conflict.line: Buffett argues 10x earnings already assumes catastrophe; Munger counters that losing the product war to Lilly is not a catastrophe scenario — it's the current scoreboard.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: Ten times earnings for a duopolist in the biggest drug category of the era. Pessimism is on sale.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: Deserved pessimism, partly. Lilly's molecule wins head-to-head and owns 60% of the US market. Cheapness against a stronger rival is a value trap's favorite costume.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: So let the pipeline referee it. CagriSema approval and a return-to-growth guidance are the tripwires. Until then, 2–3% is participation, not conviction.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: Chronic-disease franchises are as close to subscriptions as medicine gets. Second place in a duopoly this size is still a good business — just not at any size of bet.

tieredAdvice.logic: Historic-low multiple with pipeline optionality
The single most-loaded catalyst (2026 Q4)
Add only after growth guidance turns positive again

inversion: CagriSema misses or disappoints and the pipeline story deflates
GLP-1 category-level safety issue emerges
Two consecutive years of revenue decline confirm the bear case
companies.mirrorTest: Second-best player in a giant duopoly at a crisis multiple, with named catalysts and named tripwires. A defined-risk bet, not a leap of faith.

companies.name: Lululemon Athletica
companies.verdictLine: Good business + capable-enough management + an excellent price: PE 9x, 78% below its 10-year average, after a 77% drawdown. 89–92% repurchase rates say the brand is alive. The stock fell like a fad; the customer data says it isn't one. Staged buy.

duan.thesis: >90% direct-to-consumer, 58% gross margin, 30% ROIC, 89–92% repurchase rates. The premium athleisure ceiling is still high.

buffett.thesis: PE 9 versus a 10-year average of 41. From $511 to $119 — the market has pre-paid for a decade of bad news.

munger.thesis: Brand plus community is a middling moat with no patents; Alo and Vuori are genuinely eating the younger cohort.

lilu.thesis: A CEO handover is the single largest risk event a brand company can have. Wait for the new chief to prove himself before sizing up.

conflict.line: Buffett calls a 9x multiple on a 30%-ROIC brand a gift; Li Lu answers with Under Armour's ghost — brands do fall off altars, usually right after the founder-era management leaves.

debate.speaker: buffett
debate.text: Nine times earnings for a brand whose customers come back ninety percent of the time. The price already assumes decline.

debate.speaker: lilu
debate.text: Invert with me: how does this lose big? The brand loses the young — the Under Armour path. Probability isn't zero, and the CEO seat is changing hands at the worst moment.

debate.speaker: munger
debate.text: The competition is real this time. Alo and Vuori aren't Under Armour clones; they're winning the exact demographic Lululemon needs next.

debate.speaker: duan
debate.text: Ninety percent repurchase is the number I trust most in this room. Buy in stages; let the new CEO earn the rest of the position.

tieredAdvice.logic: 77% drawdown on an intact repurchase base

tieredAdvice.action: Half position, complete after new CEO's first two quarters
tieredAdvice.logic: Let the transition de-risk itself
Young-cohort share is the tripwire to watch

inversion: Brand loses the next generation to Alo/Vuori (the Under Armour path)
New CEO forces a strategy reset that stalls two years
Tariffs and North America slowdown compress margins together
companies.mirrorTest: A premium brand priced like a broken one, with the repurchase data contradicting the stock chart. The bet is on brand durability through a CEO change — staged entry pays you to find out.
